exercises.video_explanation_script: The barbell bicep curl is the fundamental bicep-building exercise. Stand with a barbell in your hands using an underhand grip, arms fully extended. Your elbows should be pinned to your sides - imagine they're glued there. From here, curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending your elbows. The key is that only your forearms move - your upper arms stay completely still. At the top, squeeze your biceps hard and think about supinating your wrists by turning your pinkies outward. Lower the weight under control, fully extending your arms at the bottom. The most common mistake is using your back or swinging the weight - if you need to do that, the weight is too heavy. Keep it strict and controlled.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Dumbbell bicep curls are a classic for a reason - they allow for natural wrist rotation which maximizes bicep activation. Stand with dumbbells at your sides. You can start with your palms facing your thighs or already facing forward. As you curl the dumbbells up, rotate your wrists outward - this is called supination and it's what your biceps are designed to do. Keep your elbows pinned to your sides the entire time. At the top, squeeze your biceps hard. Lower under control, fully extending your arms. You can do both arms at once or alternate - alternating allows better focus on each arm. The key is controlling the weight and really emphasizing that wrist rotation at the top.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Hammer curls are essential for building thick, strong arms because they target the brachialis - the muscle underneath your biceps that pushes them up and out. Stand with dumbbells at your sides, but here's the key: keep your palms facing each other in a neutral grip, thumbs pointing up. This neutral grip is maintained throughout the entire movement - no rotating. Curl the dumbbells up like you're hammering something toward the ceiling. Keep your elbows pinned at your sides and squeeze at the top. Lower under control and fully extend your arms. You should feel this on the outside of your biceps and in your forearms. Hammer curls build arm thickness and are easier on your wrists and elbows than traditional curls.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Preacher curls are the ultimate isolation exercise for your biceps. Sit at the preacher bench with your chest against the top of the pad and your upper arms resting flat on the angled surface. This setup eliminates any ability to cheat or use momentum - your biceps do all the work. Start with your arms fully extended, holding a barbell or EZ-bar. Curl the weight up toward your face, keeping your upper arms glued to the pad. Squeeze hard at the top. Lower under control, but here's important: don't hyperextend your elbows at the bottom. Stop just short of full lockout. This exercise is humbling - you'll use less weight than standing curls, but the isolation is incredible. Perfect for building that bicep peak.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Concentration curls are all about the mind-muscle connection. Sit on a bench with your legs spread wide. Lean forward and brace your working arm's elbow against your inner thigh. Let the dumbbell hang with your arm fully extended. From here, curl the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, keeping your elbow firmly pressed against your thigh. At the top, squeeze your bicep as hard as you can and hold it. This isn't about moving heavy weight - it's about feeling every inch of the movement and getting maximum contraction. Lower under control and fully extend your arm. The braced position eliminates any ability to cheat, making this one of the purest bicep isolation exercises. Perfect for finishing your arm workout.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Cable bicep curls offer a huge advantage over free weights - constant tension throughout the entire range of motion. Set the cable pulley to the lowest position and attach a straight bar or EZ-bar. Stand facing the machine, holding the bar with an underhand grip. Lean back slightly to create a stable position. From here, curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping your elbows pinned at your sides. The key difference from dumbbells is that the cable maintains tension even at full extension. You should feel your biceps working throughout the entire rep. Lower under control, resisting the cable's pull. This constant tension is excellent for building a pump and creating metabolic stress for muscle growth.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Incline dumbbell curls are one of the best exercises for building that bicep peak by targeting the long head. Set a bench to a 45-degree incline and sit with your back firmly against it. Let the dumbbells hang straight down at your sides - your arms will be behind your body plane, which creates a deep stretch in the long head of your biceps. This stretched position is what makes this exercise special. From here, curl the dumbbells up toward your shoulders, rotating your wrists as you go. Keep your back against the pad and don't let your elbows drift forward. Squeeze at the top, then lower under control back to that deep stretch. You'll need to use lighter weight than flat curls, but the stretch-mediated hypertrophy you get from this exercise is incredible for building bigger biceps.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Reverse curls are essential for building overall arm mass because they target the brachialis and forearms. Stand with a barbell using an overhand grip - palms facing down. This pronated grip is what makes it different from regular curls. From here, curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping your palms down the entire time. Your elbows stay pinned at your sides. The key is keeping your wrists strong and neutral - don't let them bend backward. You'll use much less weight than regular curls, maybe 30-50% less, and that's normal. Lower under control and fully extend your arms. This exercise builds thickness in your forearms and the brachialis muscle underneath your biceps, which pushes your biceps up and out for bigger-looking arms overall.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Spider curls are an advanced bicep exercise that really emphasizes the short head for bicep width. Instead of sitting at the preacher bench normally, you're going to lean over the top of it so your chest is against the pad and your arms hang straight down the vertical side. This creates a much more vertical arm angle than regular preacher curls. From here, curl the weight straight up toward your face, keeping your upper arms pressed against the pad. The vertical position creates maximum tension at the peak contraction. Squeeze hard at the top, then lower under control. This exercise is called spider curls because the position looks like a spider climbing up the pad. The unique angle really hammers the short head of your biceps for that width and thickness.

exercises.video_explanation_script: 21s are an advanced high-intensity technique that will set your biceps on fire. You'll perform 21 total reps broken into three phases. Start with the bar at full extension. Phase one: do 7 reps in just the bottom half of the movement - from full extension to 90 degrees where your forearms are parallel to the floor. Stop right there, don't go higher. Phase two: now do 7 reps in just the top half - from that 90-degree position to full contraction at your shoulders. Finally, phase three: do 7 complete full range reps from full extension to full contraction. That's 21 total reps without rest. Use about 60-70% of what you'd normally curl because this is brutal. The bottom half emphasizes the stretch, the top half emphasizes the squeeze, and the full reps bring it all together after your biceps are already exhausted. This is an advanced technique for breaking through plateaus.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Chin-ups are one of the absolute best exercises for building big, strong biceps while also developing your back. Hang from a pull-up bar with an underhand grip - palms facing you - hands about shoulder-width apart. Start from a full dead hang with your arms completely extended. From here, pull yourself up by driving your elbows down toward your hips. Think about pulling your chest to the bar, not just getting your chin over. The underhand grip maximizes bicep involvement compared to overhand pull-ups. Pull until your chin clearly clears the bar, squeeze at the top, then lower yourself under control back to a full dead hang. If you can't do bodyweight chin-ups yet, use a resistance band for assistance or practice negative chin-ups. Once you can do 10+ reps, add weight with a belt or vest.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Cable hammer curls combine the brachialis-building benefits of hammer curls with the constant tension of cables. Set a cable pulley to the lowest position with a rope attachment. Stand facing the machine and grab the rope ends with a neutral grip - palms facing each other, thumbs up. Lean back slightly for stability. From here, curl the rope up toward your shoulders while maintaining that neutral grip throughout. The cable creates constant tension on your brachialis and forearms, unlike dumbbells where tension drops off at the top. Keep your elbows pinned at your sides and squeeze at the top. Control the weight back down, resisting the cable's pull. The constant tension makes this excellent for building arm thickness and getting a great pump.
